MA3491 overview

MA3491 Topic Guide

Secondary Coding Topics

Prepare these after the core six: they are examinable, but less consistently visible in the local archive.

Purpose

This guide covers weight enumerators, MacWilliams' identity, perfect/MDS/self-dual ideas, repetition/check-digit examples, and a cautious BCH orientation.Exam use: Definition, dual-code relation, field equations, basis, dimension identity, orthogonality and requested enumerator convention are shown.

Question plan

  1. Identify the definition being tested.
  2. Compute a small explicit example before making a classification claim.
  3. For a MacWilliams question, identify whether the one- or two-variable enumerator convention is being used before substituting.
  4. For BCH, state the chosen roots/consecutive powers and derive g as their minimal-polynomial lcm.
  5. Question interpretation: Identify whether the prompt concerns duality, equivalence, weight enumeration or a bound, and state the exact invariant before calculating.

Formulas

Weight enumerator WC(z)=Σc∈Czwt(c). For a binary code, MacWilliams' identity is WC⊥(z)=|C|−1(1+z)nWC((1−z)/(1+z)). Perfect means sphere-packing equality; MDS means Singleton equality. C is self-dual when C=C⊥, so n=2k. A BCH generator polynomial is lcm of the minimal polynomials of its prescribed consecutive roots.Rapid recall: C^perp={x:x dot c=0 for all c in C}, dim C+dim C^perp=n; check the requested enumerator convention before applying MacWilliams.

Derivation

Enumerate codewords and group by weight to obtain W. Equality in the relevant bound gives the two classifications. For self-duality, dim C+dim C⊥=n, so equality of codes forces k=n/2. BCH roots make every codeword vanish at those roots; their minimal polynomials therefore divide g.Exam workflow: Translate the definition into a matrix nullspace, calculate over F_q, then verify dimensions and orthogonality as independent checks.

Worked example

For C={000,101,011,110}, WC(z)=1+3z2. It is not self-dual: n=3 is odd, so n=2k cannot hold. Its d=2.

Medium/hard paper-style synthesis

For binary C generated by (1,1,0,0) and (0,1,1,0), solve x1+x2=0 and x2+x3=0. Thus x1=x2=x3 and x4 is free, so C^perp=span{(1,1,1,0),(0,0,0,1)}. Both dimensions are 2 and sum to n=4; dot products with generator rows vanish.

Graduated exam bridge

1. Classify a code meeting M=qn−d+1. Check: it is MDS; this alone does not say perfect.

2. Compute a weight enumerator from a supplied G, then outline the data required to construct a BCH generator polynomial. Check: enumerate all qk codewords; name the field, length, designed distance/roots and minimal polynomials.

Hard paper-style synthesis

Paper-style synthesis: compute the weight enumerator of C. Check codewords are 0000,1100,0110,1010, with weights 0,2,2,2, so W_C(z)=1+3z^2; use the convention requested if two variables are used.

Practice question - enumerator and duality [8 marks]

Task. For C={0000,1100,0110,1010}, find WC(z) and decide whether C is self-dual over F2. [8 marks]

Demand diagnosis and fastest route: enumerate all supplied words, then compare C with C⊥, not just dimensions.

Worked answer: The weights are 0,2,2,2, so WC(z)=1+3z2. C has dimension 2 because 1100 and 0110 are independent. Their dot product is 1, so C is not self-orthogonal; consequently it cannot equal C⊥, even though both have dimension 2 in length 4. Dimension equality is necessary for self-duality but not sufficient.

Topic-specific trap: never infer self-dual solely from n=2k.

Mistakes

  • Confusing perfect with MDS.
  • Counting only generator rows in a weight enumerator.
  • Claiming a BCH construction without specifying roots or a splitting field.
  • Recovery rule: Orthogonal complement depends on the field's dot product; integer arithmetic can give the wrong nullspace.

Checklist

  • I know the three equality definitions.
  • I can enumerate a small weight enumerator.
  • I can give a qualified BCH construction outline.
  • Final 60-second audit: Definition, field equations, basis, dimension identity, orthogonality and requested enumerator convention are shown.

Past-paper note

Weight enumerators appeared in 2022/23, 2023/24 and 2025/26. The 2025/26 paper paired them with a cyclic code, asked for the dual code's enumerator, and introduced MacWilliams' identity. Weight enumerators are therefore recurring secondary material; MacWilliams is a new one-paper extension. BCH is official scope yet not a stable local-paper pattern.
